prompt: Create a diagram of a Lambda-based API with three handlers (create, get, search) behind API Gateway, using DynamoDB, S3 and OpenSearch. OpenSearch is kept up to date by an async Lambda listening to the DynamoDB stream. Lay it out in clear tiers.
A classic three-tier web app: an Application Load Balancer in front of an ECS (Fargate) service, backed by an Aurora database and an ElastiCache cache. Include the user.

Order events flow through EventBridge to two consumers: an email notifier (Lambda plus SNS) and an analytics writer (Lambda plus an S3 data lake). Failed events land in an SQS dead-letter queue. Show asynchronous flows as async.

Three microservices (catalog, checkout, identity) behind one API gateway, each service with its own API lambda and its own database. Provide a landscape view plus a zoomed view of the checkout service. Give the services descriptions so their cards read well.
Clickstream data pipeline: a Kinesis stream feeds a Lambda transformer that lands data in an S3 data lake; Glue catalogs it and analysts query it with Athena. The analysts are people.
Serverless image pipeline: uploads land in an S3 bucket, which asynchronously triggers a Lambda that calls Rekognition for labels, writes metadata to DynamoDB, and notifies subscribers via SNS.

A partner company's system (external, not ours) calls our public API Gateway; each request runs a Step Functions workflow that orchestrates a validation Lambda and a billing Lambda which writes to Aurora. Mark the partner system as external.

A payments service: an API Lambda, a tokenizer Lambda, a card vault on DynamoDB, and a settlement worker draining an SQS queue asynchronously. Tag everything that touches card data with #pci, and add a view that highlights the PCI surface with a note explaining where tokens are stored.

Realtime ML inference: client apps call an API Gateway and Lambda front end that queries a SageMaker endpoint; features come from a DynamoDB feature store. A nightly batch job asynchronously retrains the model using training data in S3.

A legacy on-premises ERP system (no cloud icon — it is not an AWS service) feeds a sync worker Lambda over an asynchronous link; the worker writes to an RDS database used by a new admin dashboard web app, which administrators (people) use.

Draw our hybrid estate: an on-premises data centre running a legacy Oracle-style ERP (no cloud icon) and the operators who use it, feeding an AWS cloud where an ingestion Lambda writes to an Aurora database. Put a boundary around the on-prem side and around the AWS side, and mark the database's VPC separately.

A checkout path: API Gateway to a cart Lambda, cart to a payment Lambda, payment writes to DynamoDB and asynchronously publishes to an SQS queue that a fulfilment worker drains. Number the steps of the checkout journey so a reader can follow the order of events, and show a legend.

Five Lambda handlers (create, read, update, delete, search) all write to one DynamoDB table behind an API Gateway. The five lines converging on the table look like spaghetti — make them share a single trunk into the table instead.

A payments platform: API Lambda, tokenizer Lambda, card vault on DynamoDB, an analytics Lambda and a Redshift warehouse. Tag everything in PCI scope, then give me two views — the full picture, and an auditor's view that shows only the PCI-tagged parts.

Our stack has nothing to do with AWS: a Next.js frontend, a NestJS API, PostgreSQL, Redis for caching, Kafka for events, and Grafana watching it all. Developers push to GitHub which deploys to Kubernetes. Use the real product logos.

Document our order platform end to end: customers hit a CloudFront-fronted storefront, which calls an API Gateway routing to catalog, orders and payments services, each with its own Lambda and database. Orders publishes events to EventBridge that a fulfilment worker consumes. Everything except the storefront runs inside a production VPC. Tag the payments path as sensitive. Give me a landscape view and a zoomed view of the orders service.

Draw our Azure web application: customers reach it through Azure Front Door, which fronts an App Service running the web tier. The App Service reads and writes Azure SQL, caches in Redis, pulls secrets from Key Vault, and reports telemetry to Application Insights. Show the telemetry as asynchronous.

Our Azure estate, with the network boundaries drawn: a virtual network contains a private subnet with an AKS cluster and a Container Registry it pulls images from. Azure SQL sits outside the subnet but inside the same virtual network. An Application Gateway sits in front of the whole thing, and everything lives inside one Azure subscription. Show the subscription, the virtual network and the subnet as separate boundaries.

Show how an order travels through our Azure system, numbered step by step: the shopper hits API Management, which calls an Azure Function. The function writes the order to Cosmos DB and then publishes a message to Service Bus, which a second function picks up to handle fulfilment. Number the path an order takes so I can walk a room through it.

We are mid-migration and I need one picture of it. On-premises we still run a PostgreSQL database and a RabbitMQ broker on our own hardware. In Azure we have an AKS cluster running the new services and Azure SQL as the target database. A sync job copies from the old Postgres to Azure SQL nightly, asynchronously. Use real product logos for the on-prem software and Azure icons for the Azure side, and put a boundary around each side.
